topic: How does a hash table with chaining handle collisions?
title: Hash Tables and Collisions

scenes.narration: A hash table turns each key into a bucket number. Ours has 5 buckets and uses the key mod 5. The keys 12 and 7 both landed in bucket 2, a collision, so they share a chain.
scenes.caption: Jump straight to the right bucket

scenes.narration: 3 mod 5 is 3, so the key 3 goes straight into the empty bucket 3.
scenes.caption: insert 3: bucket 3

scenes.narration: 17 mod 5 is 2, another collision. 17 joins the end of the chain in bucket 2, after 12 and 7.
scenes.caption: insert 17: bucket 2

scenes.narration: To find 7 we only look in bucket 2 and walk its chain: 12, then 7. Found, without touching any other bucket.
scenes.caption: search 7

scenes.narration: Deleting 12 also starts at bucket 2. We remove it from the chain, which now holds 7 and 17. The size is 3.
scenes.caption: delete 12

scenes.narration: 10 mod 5 is 0, and bucket 0 is empty, so we know at once that 10 is not in the table.
scenes.caption: search 10: not found

scenes.narration: A good hash function spreads keys evenly, so chains stay short and lookups stay fast.
scenes.caption: Summary
points: The hash picks the bucket: key mod 5
O(1) on average, O(n) if every key collides

quiz.question: A table with 4 buckets holds 5 and 9. We insert 13, using key mod 4. Which keys are in its bucket?
quiz.explanation: 5, 9 and 13 all leave remainder 1 when divided by 4.

quiz.question: A table with 7 buckets holds 10 and 3. Into which bucket does 24 go, using key mod 7?
